title: The hypertrophy series: utilizing tonnage for muscle growth
summary: The practical follow-up on tonnage. NH recommends programs built on repeatable sets, with static back-off sets, the same weight across sets and small rep drop-offs. He talks about tonnage sacrifice, why minimalism hurts intermediates, and why bodybuilders should chase slow, unbroken tonnage growth rather than powerlifting-style peaks, blocks and deloads.
claims: Patience, measured by tonnage accumulated over time within the right intensity windows, is the objective route to getting bigger
Use programs that encourage set repetition: for many lifts choose a slightly lighter weight that allows more reps and sets
When adding weight, the rep range should not shrink dramatically; that is acceptable only for the strength hook, e.g. 3 sets of 3-4 back down to 1 set of 2
Back-off sets and variations should be static or vary by only one or two sets, e.g. 3-4 back-off sets
Static schemes like 5x5 and 3x5 force conservative weight jumps because you must repeat the effort next week
He used to get 4 reps on a first set but only 1-2 on the next after 3-4 minutes of rest, which hurt tonnage accumulation, so he worked to fix it
He uses the same weight on every scheduled set, never pyramiding, and expects reps like 10, then 9-8, then 8-7
Missing those rep targets counts, for him, as a failure to accumulate the damage he wanted
Tonnage sacrifice: do not fear cutting work; the bigger your weekly tonnage, the smaller the percentage any cut represents
Minimalism is bad for late novices and intermediates because any cut is too large a share of their training
The strength hook is the one cornerstone you never cut; everything after it is expendable
Time is undervalued on YouTube Fitness: the same training for 2 years versus 10 years gives massively different results
Strength and hypertrophy blocks are unnecessary and can be detrimental for bodybuilders
Powerlifters peak, drop and peak higher, which works for strength but not tonnage, which is why their strength does not match their size
Bodybuilders should progress slowly and without stopping; powerlifters will always be stronger, but the bodybuilder's tonnage and size go further
Bouncing between hypertrophy and strength training is like living with divorced parents; it should all be hypertrophy, with strength work existing only to drive tonnage
Deloads and blocks make sense for powerlifters but not bodybuilders; breaks that cause big tonnage dips make your progress yo-yo
Rather than thinking about strength, intensity or volume, think only about tonnage, and the rest follows
